# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When I receive my three crates, I will calculate my true total value accurately and use it as my baseline.

I will declare my true value when I'm ahead, tied, or only moderately behind (within 20 points with 3+ rounds left). This keeps me safe from the -40 spot check penalty and builds a foundation for incremental gains.

When I'm significantly behind in the mid-game (more than 20 points back in rounds 3-5), I will declare 5-10 points above my true total. This creates upside through the main route (30% duty) while staying conservative enough that a spot check penalty doesn't eliminate my chances.

In the final round, if I'm behind by 10+ points, I will declare 10 points above my true total. The single-round penalty is survivable and the upside swing is worth the risk when a catch doesn't end the game.

I will never declare so high that the difference is more than 10-15 points from my true total on main route, since the spot check penalty of -40 points plus recomputed duty at true value becomes catastrophic.

I will always verify that my declared value is at least as high as my heaviest crate, since that's what the dockhand will weigh. If uncertain, I'll round up slightly to protect against flags.

## Route Selection

I will always take the main route unless I am deliberately understating my value by 15+ points. The main route's 30% duty is predictable and manageable even with modest overstatement (5-10 points).

I will take the night route only when I declare significantly below my true total (at least 15+ points under). The night route's confiscation of my smallest crate means I only benefit if I'm already hiding value; otherwise the penalty outweighs the 15% duty savings.

I should never take the night route defensively when I'm close to my true value. The confiscation is a real cost that doesn't pair well with near-honest declarations.

## Position-Aware Adjustments

When I'm ahead or within 10 points in the early to mid-game (rounds 1-3), I will play conservatively: true declarations and main routes. Building a comfortable lead through consistency is safer than chasing with risky declarations.

When I'm 15-30 points behind with 3+ rounds left, I will declare 7-10 points above my true total and take main. This creates enough upside to catch up incrementally without overcommitting.

When I'm behind by more than 30 points with only 1-2 rounds left, I can afford to declare 15+ points above my true total on main route. The one-time penalty for being caught is acceptable compared to certain second place.

## What Worked This Episode

Honest declarations kept me competitive throughout and avoided early penalties. I stayed within 1 point of the leader going into the final round, which is a winning position.

The late-game aggression in rounds 5-6 (declaring 70 with true 56, then 88 with true 78) was partly effective but inconsistent. Round 5's declaration of 70 when true was 56 overextended; I should have declared 61-65. Round 6's declaration of 88 when true was 78 was more justifiable in the final round but I got lucky not to be caught.

## What Didn't Work This Episode

I stayed too conservative in the middle rounds when I was 10-15 points behind. Rounds 2-3 I should have been slightly more aggressive (5-7 points above true) to close the gap faster rather than hoping for naturally good hands.

I didn't adjust quickly enough to Mirren's lead. By round 4-5, the gap was hard to close, which is when I made the leap to more aggressive declarations. Earlier aggression in round 3 would have been better timed.

# HARBOR CUSTOMS PLAYBOOK

## DECLARING

When I see my three crates, I will calculate my true total value immediately.

When deciding my declaration, I will identify my heaviest crate first—this is my hard floor. I cannot declare below it without risking a -40 penalty that will crater my round.

When I'm ahead or tied in score, I will declare my true value or slightly below to lock in safe points.

When I'm behind in score, I will declare close to my true value but not recklessly above it. Aggressive declarations help me catch up, but flagging costs me more than caution gains me.

When comparing routes mathematically at declaration time, I will calculate both outcomes:
- Main: full crate value minus 30% duty
- Night: crate value minus smallest crate minus 15% duty

When the math shows night is better, I will note it now, but I should default to main unless I have a compelling reason.

I will stop declaring overly conservative values mid-tournament. Round 2 showed me declaring 35 on crates worth 64 was too timid and cost me ground against the field.

In a close final round where I'm within striking distance (1-2 points behind), declaring my true value is correct. It maximizes my expected points without overextending. The field will declare near their true values too.

## ROUTING

When I route to main, I am choosing consistency and full crate retention.

When I route to night, I am accepting the loss of my smallest crate in exchange for lower duty. This is only worth it if my smallest crate is much smaller than my duty savings.

When the field has gone all-main for several rounds and I'm behind, I should not assume everyone will stay conservative. I should position for what helps me catch up rather than what feels "safe."

When I declare moderately high (50+), main route is my default because I've already committed to a visible bid; night route then becomes a bet that the field won't read aggression into my declaration.

I will avoid vague reasoning like "stay consistent with my round 3 strategy" when routing. Each route decision stands alone. I should recalculate the duty math fresh each time.

When I declare a value close to my true total on modest holdings (40-70 range), main route is almost always the correct default. Night route sacrifices real crate value for minor duty savings that don't materially change the outcome.

## SCORING STRATEGY

When I fall behind early, I will lean into higher declarations in later rounds rather than retreat further behind.

When the final round arrives and I'm in second place within a few points, I will declare close to my true total rather than leaving value on the table hoping for safety.

I will track not just my score but my position relative to each opponent. Being 1 point behind with 1 round left means I need to maximize that final round, not protect it.

At the end of a 6-round tournament, the margin is tight. Every round matters equally. I should not treat round 6 differently from round 5 in terms of boldness—the only thing that changes is the availability of future rounds to recover in.

I should expect the field to declare near true value when I do. Declaring 45 when my true total is 45, in a field where others have been declaring 60-80, is rational for my position but won't necessarily give me an edge over Mirren if she also declares near her true value. Final round outcomes are largely determined by the luck of the draw, not the declaration strategy.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

**On Declaration:**

When I see my three crates, I will declare their true total value. Declaring honestly gives me maximum flexibility on route choice and avoids the -40 penalty risk if my largest crate is checked. The penalty is severe enough that the safety of an honest declaration outweighs any marginal gain from strategic understatement.

**On Route Selection:**

When choosing between main and night, I will take the main route as my default. The main route's duty of 0.30 is higher but guarantees I keep all three crates. The night route saves duty but costs me my smallest crate permanently—a real loss I cannot recover.

I should consider night route only if:
- I am significantly ahead in the standings (by 30+ points or more)
- The round-to-round variance is worth the permanent loss of my smallest crate value
- There are multiple rounds remaining to make up any shortfall

Since I stayed in second place throughout this episode and never had a decisive lead, taking main every time was correct. The night route never justified itself given my position.

**On Catching Up:**

When I am behind in points, declaring high does not close the gap—it just increases risk without proportional reward. The scoring structure means even perfect declarations on main route only yield a few dozen points per round. I cannot "catch up aggressively" in the final round. I should focus on consistent, risk-managed scoring throughout, not heroic swings in the endgame.

In the final round, safety matters more than upside. A guaranteed 20-30 points beats a risky 35-40 points when the game is nearly over.

**On Consistent Performance:**

This game rewards steady honesty more than clever deception. Declare true value, choose your route based on standings position and risk tolerance, and collect your points. The crate distribution determines the gap between players; my execution should minimize regret, not chase variance.

I finished with 316 points by executing this strategy faithfully. That total reflects the cards dealt to me, not flaws in my approach.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When declaring, calculate your true total crate value first. This is your anchor.

The -40 penalty for underdeclaring (when your largest crate exceeds your declaration) is severe. To avoid it, I must declare at least as much as my largest crate. This is a hard floor, not negotiable.

Beyond the floor, I have a choice: declare true value, or declare lower (but still safe). Declaring true value is usually correct because:
- It avoids the flag penalty entirely
- It signals consistency to the table
- The duty calculation is straightforward and predictable
- I stay anchored to what I actually hold

Study the table's declaration patterns. If declarations cluster in a range (e.g., 52–81 across rounds), stay within or slightly above that range. Outliers draw no advantage and risk looking suspicious.

When I have weak crates (all small values), I can declare conservatively because my largest crate is still small; the floor is not onerous. When I have strong crates, my largest crate is large, so the floor is higher—but I have the value to back it up, so declaring true value is still the right call.

I should not artificially suppress declarations below my true value just to avoid "standing out." The table's declarations vary round to round naturally. A declaration of 68 or 85 is not an outlier when the range is 40–81.

Adjust declarations based on position only if I'm far behind with rounds remaining. Otherwise, maximize my own score each round rather than chasing the leader. Consistent, honest declarations compound better than variance-chasing.

## Route Selection

When I declare my true value and my crates are solid, the main route is the default. It is simple, predictable, and rarely wrong.

To decide whether night route wins instead, I must do the math:
- Main route: (true total) - 0.30×(declared value) = net points
- Night route: (true total - smallest crate) - 0.15×(declared value) = net points

Night route wins only when the crate I lose is small enough that the duty savings (0.15×declared vs. 0.30×declared) more than compensate for losing it.

Example: declared 62, crates 13, 13, 36 (true total 62)
- Main: 62 - floor(0.30 × 62) = 62 - 18 = 44
- Night: (62 - 13) - floor(0.15 × 62) = 49 - 9 = 40
- Main wins. Stick with it.

Example: declared 91, crates 15, 37, 39 (true total 91)
- Main: 91 - floor(0.30 × 91) = 91 - 27 = 64
- Night: (91 - 15) - floor(0.15 × 91) = 76 - 13 = 63
- Main wins again.

I found that main route was correct in every round I played. I should not assume night route is "rarely" correct—assume it is wrong until the math proves otherwise. Do the calculation every time. Most of the time, main will win.

In the final round, default to main route unless the math clearly favors night. The variance is not worth chasing when the game is ending.

## Scoring and Positioning

I finished second place overall (271 points) using honest, steady declarations and main route almost exclusively. This strategy works. Do not abandon it.

When I deviate from this baseline, have a reason. Declaring 85 in round 5 when my true value was 91 was slightly conservative, but it kept me safe and competitive—I ended up only 1 point behind the leader going into the final round. Consistency and safety compound better than optimizing every round for a fractional edge.

Do not obsess over other players' declarations or positions mid-game. Focus on maximizing my own score each round. Chasing leaders with reckless declarations costs more than it gains. Krek and Odalie both scored significantly less than me despite higher declarations in some rounds; they took bigger risks and did not get rewarded.

Review my final tally: I was within 1 point of the leader and beat two other players decisively. The playbook works.
